name: BoolQ
description: BoolQ is a reading comprehension dataset of naturally occurring yes/no questions. Each example consists of a question, a paragraph from a Wikipedia article, the title of the article, and an answer (yes or no). The questions are gathered from anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine and paired with Wikipedia passages. The dataset contains 16,000 examples split into a 9.4k train set, 3.2k dev set, and 3.2k test set.
creator: Christopher Clark, Kenton Lee, Ming-Wei Chang, Tom Kwiatkowski, Michael Collins, Kristina Toutanova
publisher: Google AI Language / University of Washington
citeAs: Clark, C., Lee, K., Chang, M.-W., Kwiatkowski, T., Collins, M., & Toutanova, K. (2019). BoolQ: Exploring the Surprising Difficulty of Natural Yes/No Questions. arXiv:1905.10044.
rai:dataCollection: Questions are gathered from anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine. Queries likely to be yes/no questions are heuristically identified by selecting queries where the first word is in a manually constructed set of indicator words and are of sufficient length. Questions are only kept if a Wikipedia page is returned as one of the first five results. The question and Wikipedia page are then given to a human annotator for further processing. Annotators label question/article pairs in a three-step process: (1) deciding if the question is good (comprehensible, unambiguous, requesting factual information) before seeing the Wikipedia page; (2) finding a passage within the document that contains enough information to answer the question; (3) marking whether the answer is 'yes' or 'no'. 13k questions were gathered from this pipeline and combined with an additional 3k yes/no questions from the Natural Questions (NQ) training set.
rai:dataCollectionType: Web API, Manual Human Curator, Secondary Data analysis
rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Annotators can mark questions as 'not answerable' if the Wikipedia article does not contain the requested information.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine paired with Wikipedia pages returned as one of the first five search results. An additional 3k yes/no questions were sourced from the Natural Questions (NQ) training set.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Questions from NQ are always placed in the train set. The dataset is split into a 3.2k dev set, 3.2k test set, and 9.4k train set. Each question is paired with the selected passage instead of the entire document to reduce ambiguity and keep input size manageable.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Queries are heuristically filtered to identify yes/no questions by selecting those where the first word is in a manually constructed set of indicator words {'did', 'do', 'does', 'is', 'are', 'was', 'were', 'have', 'has', 'can', 'could', 'will', 'would'} and are of sufficient length. Only questions where a Wikipedia page is returned as one of the first five search results are kept. Questions marked as not good or not answerable by annotators are excluded. Only questions marked as having a yes/no answer are used.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators label question/article pairs in a three-step process. First, they decide if the question is 'good' (comprehensible, unambiguous, and requesting factual information) before seeing the Wikipedia page. Next, for good questions, annotators find a passage within the document that contains enough information to answer the question, and can mark questions as 'not answerable' if the Wikipedia article does not contain the requested information. Finally, annotators mark whether the question's answer is 'yes' or 'no'. The dataset uses singly-annotated examples in the training/dev/test sets. Annotation quality was assessed by having three of the authors label 110 randomly chosen examples; disagreements were resolved by mutual agreement to create 'gold-standard' labels, achieving 90% accuracy compared to the gold-standard.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Three of the authors labelled 110 randomly chosen examples to assess annotation quality. If there was a disagreement, the authors conferred and selected a single answer by mutual agreement ('gold-standard' labels). The answer annotations reached 90% accuracy compared to the gold-standard labels. Of the cases where the answer annotation differed from the gold-standard, six were ambiguous or debatable cases, and five were errors where the annotator misunderstood the passage. Since agreement was sufficiently high, singly-annotated examples were used in the training/dev/test sets.
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset has been noted to have been updated since some analyses were carried out (footnote 4 mentions the dataset was updated after the inference type analysis). No formal versioning or deprecation policy is described.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Questions are derived from anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is directly related to the practical end-task of answering user yes/no questions, which has applications in question answering systems and natural language understanding.
rai:dataBiases: 'Yes' answers are slightly more common (62.31% in the train set). The Y/N MS Marco heuristically constructed dataset is class imbalanced with 80% 'yes' answers. QuAC is also highly class imbalanced with 80% 'yes' answers.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset contains only yes/no questions and may not generalize to other question types. The inference type analysis may be slightly out-of-date as the dataset was updated after that analysis was carried out. The dataset is Wikipedia-based, which may present domain shift issues when applied to other domains. Questions from NQ are restricted to the train set, which may affect distribution across splits.
rai:dataUseCases: Training, development (validation), and testing of reading comprehension and natural language inference models. The dataset is intended for use in yes/no question answering, studying transfer learning for NLP tasks, and benchmarking models on naturally occurring inferential questions. It can also be used to study entailment-like inference in paragraph-level contexts.
